analysis.one_liner: Would have blocked three rules strengthening Endangered Species Act protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after introduction and referral to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, it sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In June 2023, the federal wildlife agencies proposed rules to strengthen how the Endangered Species Act is carried out — including how agencies consult before actions that could harm listed species, and how species get protected and habitat designated. This bill would have forced the agencies to withdraw those proposed rules and forbidden them from ever finalizing or enforcing them. It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and landowners in industries constrained by endangered species rules — oil, gas, and mining operators on federal land, timber and grazing interests, and developers — would gain if the rules were withdrawn, because weaker consultation and habitat rules mean fewer reviews, restrictions, and delays before projects can proceed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Resource developers and Western land users

how_it_helps.text: It would have canceled the June 2023 proposed rules revising how federal agencies consult with wildlife agencies before actions that may affect endangered species, easing that review burden.
It would have canceled the proposed rule covering how species get listed as endangered and how critical habitat gets designated, keeping the existing, less protective listing process in place.
It barred the wildlife agencies from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing any of the three rules, so no replacement through normal rulemaking would have been possible.

analysis.who_pays: Wildlife and the public would bear the cost: less protection for threatened species and their habitat, weaker environmental review of federal and federally permitted projects, and loss of the public's normal chance to weigh in on the rules through the comment process.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wildlife and ordinary Americans who value it

drawbacks.text: Blocking the rules would have left the weaker, 2019-era Endangered Species Act regulations in place, meaning fewer protections for threatened species and looser reviews before federal actions harm habitat — a cost that falls on wildlife and on the public lands and fisheries many Americans use.

Rather than proposing changes through the public comment process, the bill would have legislated the rules out of existence wholesale, cutting off the agencies' ability to update how the Endangered Species Act is applied.
With less environmental review up front, conflicts over endangered species would more likely surface late in development projects, creating uncertainty for builders rather than reducing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit would go almost entirely to businesses that want fewer endangered-species constraints; the cost would fall on wildlife and on the public's ability to manage federal lands and fisheries through the normal rulemaking process. The underlying agencies had proposed the rules through the standard public comment process, and this bill would have overridden that with a one-time legislative cancellation [S2]. For ordinary people the bill offered little upside; its main effect would be to reduce environmental review in places where resource development and wildlife habitat overlap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 14, 2023, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
That referral was the last action of any kind: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill would have ordered the wildlife agencies to withdraw three proposed rules published in the Federal Register on June 22, 2023, and barred them from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing any of them.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Endangered Species Act protections in the proposed rules were not legislated away, so the public's existing environmental safeguards stand and resource-development interests did not get the rollback they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wildlife protections stood; the rollback failed

for.name: Cynthia Lummis
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to force withdrawal of the three Endangered Species Act rules.

for.name: 17 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all from states heavy in federal-land energy, mining, and grazing activity.

against.name: Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill, leaving it stuck at the referral stage through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, mining, and other resource development on federal land
industries.note: Endangered species listings and habitat designations can restrict access to federal land and trigger lengthy consultation reviews. Killing the proposed rules would have kept those constraints lighter, lowering compliance costs for developers in Western states.

industries.industry: Agriculture, grazing, and timber interests in species habitat
industries.note: The same rules shape habitat designations and protections for threatened species on working lands. Weaker rules mean fewer restrictions on grazing, logging, and farming operations.

industries.industry: Wildlife conservation and environmental protection interests
industries.note: The bill would have canceled rules the conservation community had sought to restore protections weakened in 2019, making permanent the lighter-touch regime those groups were trying to reverse.
